learningObjective: Design a golden test for a custom kernel by choosing an appropriate reference implementation, deterministic inputs, and tolerance schema.

canonicalClaims.claim: A robust golden test uses (a) an independent, high-precision reference implementation, (b) deterministic inputs (fixed seed) to make failures reproducible, and (c) tolerance schedules matched to the numeric dtype of the implementation under test.
conditions: The kernel implementation is being validated for correctness.
The test runs in CI where reproducibility is required.
nonImplications: Does not imply CPU/FP64 references are always feasible.
Does not imply random-input differential testing is bad; it complements golden tests.

misconceptions.claim: Using an older version of the same kernel as reference is best.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Same-family references can share bugs; independent references are stronger correctness signals.

misconceptions.claim: Golden tests should always use strict FP32 tolerance regardless of the dtype under test.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Applying FP32/FP64 tolerance to BF16/FP16 kernels causes false failures without adding correctness signal.

misconceptions.claim: Random inputs each run maximize CI value.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Non-deterministic failures are painful to debug; fixed seeds should be used for golden tests.

misconceptions.claim: End-to-end accuracy replaces per-kernel golden testing.
misconceptions.whyWrong: E2E accuracy is coarse and often insensitive to kernel-level bugs that cancel or mask.
